| | |
|---|---|
| **Script** | `code/5_ps_model.r` |
| **In** | `data/fbs_mockup_cohort.xlsx`, one row per patient |
| **Out** | `output/ps_cohort.rds`, the cohort with the propensity score, the weight and common support |

This chapter leaves the trial. A propensity score answers a question about patients who were **not** randomised, so it needs a different data set. The cohort is a mock-up made for teaching. No real patient is involved.

## The question and the cohort

| | |
|---|---|
| **Question** | Does drug B lower FBS at month 6 more than drug A? |
| **Design** | Retrospective cohort. The doctor chose the drug. |
| **Patients** | 600, one row each. Drug A 346, drug B 254. |
| **Outcome** | `fbs_m6`, fasting blood sugar at month 6 (mg/dL) |
| **Confounders** | Age, sex, BMI, diabetes duration, FBS at month 0 |

The doctor chose drug B more often for patients whose diabetes looked worse. So the two groups differ before the drug is even started. This is confounding by indication. A plain comparison of month 6 FBS mixes the effect of the drug with the effect of who got it.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 6
flowchart LR
  C["Confounders<br/>age, sex, BMI,<br/>DM duration, FBS month 0"] --> T["Drug<br/>A or B"]
  C --> Y["FBS<br/>month 6"]
  T --> Y
```

The propensity score (PS) is each patient's probability of getting drug B, given the confounders. Patients with the same PS are comparable, whichever drug they actually got.

| Script | Job |
|---|---|
| 5 (this chapter) | Build the PS, the weights and common support |
| 6 (next chapter) | Check that the weights balance the confounders |
| 7 | Estimate the effect of drug B |

## Step 3: the propensity score model

A logistic regression of the drug on the confounders.

| Goes into the PS model | Stays out |
|---|---|
| Variables that made the doctor choose B **and** change FBS at month 6 | The outcome, `fbs_m6` |
| Age, sex, BMI, diabetes duration, FBS at month 0 | Anything measured after the drug was started |

The PS describes who got which drug, not what happened afterwards. So the outcome is never in this model.

```{r}
#| label: psmodel-step-3
```

## Step 4: each patient's propensity score

`predict()` with `type = "response"` gives a probability between 0 and 1. Without it, `predict()` gives the log odds.

```{r}
#| label: psmodel-step-4
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(dplyr::select(df, id, treatment, age, fbs_m0, ps))
```

## Step 5: the weights, ATE

Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Each patient is weighted by the probability of the drug they **actually** got.

| Patient got | Weight | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Drug B | $1 / \text{PS}$ | PS = 0.2, so the weight is 5 |
| Drug A | $1 / (1 - \text{PS})$ | PS = 0.2, so the weight is 1.25 |

A patient on drug B with a PS of 0.2 was unusual for B, so stands in for 5 patients. A patient on drug A with the same PS was typical for A, so stands in for little more than one.

This weight answers the average treatment effect (ATE), namely everyone on drug B compared with everyone on drug A.

```{r}
#| label: psmodel-step-5
```

## Step 6: overlap, the PS of each group

| What to look for | Why |
|---|---|
| Drug B sits to the right of drug A | Confounding by indication. B went to the sicker patients. |
| The two histograms still overlap | Where only one group exists, nobody can be compared. This is the positivity assumption. |


## Step 7: common support

Common support is the PS range where both groups have patients. It runs from the larger of the two minimums to the smaller of the two maximums.

```{r}
#| label: psmodel-step-7
```

Common support runs from `r round(cs_low, 2)` to `r round(cs_high, 2)`. `r nrow(off_support)` patients fall outside it, and they stay in `off_support` to look at. The column `comsup` marks each patient, so a later analysis can keep only those inside.
